name: Lower lateral cartilage repositioning

lead: Lower lateral cartilage (LLC) repositioning is a nasal tip surgery in which the lower lateral cartilages, which shape the tip and nostrils, are freed and moved to a new position. People seek it to refine a bulbous or under-projected tip, lengthen a short nose, or improve tip symmetry.

Published work includes a prospective study that used 3D imaging to measure tip volume changes after LLC repositioning in patients with bulbous tips, and case series in cleft lip nasal deformity and in short noses in Asian patients.

paras: Surgeons usually operate through an open or closed rhinoplasty approach, separate the lateral crus from surrounding attachments, and reposition it, often with sutures and sometimes a columellar strut or cartilage grafts from the septum or ear. Recovery follows standard rhinoplasty timelines, with swelling taking many months to settle.

Risks are those of rhinoplasty in general: swelling, asymmetry, breathing problems and the possibility of revision surgery, which the literature puts at roughly 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties. Outcomes depend on anatomy, skin thickness and surgeon experience.

angle.text: Surgeons reposition the tip cartilages to give a bulbous or droopy tip a more defined shape or to lengthen a short nose. The change is made to the cartilage framework itself rather than the skin.

lead: Lower lateral cartilage repositioning is a rhinoplasty technique in which the alar (lower lateral) cartilages are repositioned to change the shape, projection or rotation of the nasal tip [1][2]. In looksmaxxing and surgical discussions it is a tip-refinement option: moving the lateral crura can narrow a bulbous tip, adjust its angle, or add length and mobility to a short nose.

Published reports cover several uses. A prospective study measured nasal tip volume with 3D imaging in patients with bulbous tips and cephalically oriented lower lateral cartilages who underwent repositioning [1]. Plastic surgeons also describe LLC repositioning combined with ear cartilage grafts to correct short noses in Asian patients [2] and with strut and graft techniques for cleft lip nasal deformity [3][4]. A 35-year single-surgeon review examined how often and why the lateral crura were repositioned [5].
infobox: Columellar strut, tip sutures, ear or septal cartilage grafts [2][3]

paras: The lower lateral cartilages form the tip and flare of the nostrils, with medial, intermediate and lateral crura; the lateral crura are mobile [6]. In LLC repositioning, the lateral crus is separated from its retaining attachments (except sometimes at the footplate) and brought to a new position, then held with sutures or support grafts [2][3].

The technique is described for bulbous tips with cephalically oriented cartilages [1], for lengthening short noses and increasing tip mobility in Asian rhinoplasty [2], and in secondary corrections of unilateral cleft lip nasal deformity [3][4]. Surgeons performing it commonly combine it with a columellar strut and cartilage grafts [2][3].

The 3D imaging study reported on nasal tip volume changes after repositioning in patients with bulbous tips [1]. The Asian short-nose report classified deformities into three subtypes and described its combined approach [2]. A 62-patient series used LLC repositioning with a Medpor strut and ear cartilage onlay in cleft lip nasal deformity [3]. A trial registration describes a separate approach to unilateral cleft nasal deformity using a flap and cartilage graft [7].

General rhinoplasty literature reports revision rates of roughly 5 to 20 percent, and complications including asymmetry and functional breathing problems [6]. Swelling can take a year or more to resolve [6].

A prospective clinical study used 3D imaging to analyse nasal tip volume after LLC repositioning in patients with bulbous tips [1]. Case series describe outcomes in Asian short-nose correction [2] and cleft lip nasal deformity [3][4][5].
